paper_title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A CNC machining program is the end of long chain of decisions. From CAD model of the part, CAM programmer chooses the operations for each feature and their order, the cutters, and the speeds and feeds; chooses the sides from which to approach the stock; and generates and simulates the toolpaths. The first choices draw on process knowledge. The rest is three-dimensional geometric reasoning on the boundary representation (B-rep) of the part, and it must be precise: toolpath off by fraction of millimetre gouges the part or leaves material behind. Computer-aided process planning (CAPP) has aimed to automate this chain for decades, yet in practice it still relies on human experts [4, 49]. Language models add process knowledge to this problem, but existing approaches either leave the geometry unchecked or hand it to the model. LLM process planners produce operation sequences, tools and cutting parameters [8, 19, 29] but stop before toolpaths, so their plans are never executed against the part. Other work has the model write G-code directly [3, 33, 45], and CNCGEN learns operations and toolpaths from B-rep models at the cost of large machining training set [57]. Given part, frontier model can also write and run its own geometry and toolpath code; we call this code-writing frontier agent and use it as our main baseline. In this setting, coordinates, offsets and swept volumes become the models task, and single wrong number yields program that runs but machines the wrong part. We argue that machining decisions and their geometric execution call for different machinery. Choosing the operation for feature, the cutter and how aggressively to cut is matter of process knowledge, where language model is useful. Generating toolpaths, predicting the material they remove and measuring the result are geometric computations done by algorithms; the model sets only operation-level parameters such as the tool, the finishing allowance and the depth of cut, and never computes coordinates, offsets or swept volumes. Relieved of this numerical work, locally hosted, mid-sized open model should suffice, so proprietary parts need not be sent to an outside provider; our experiments test this. We introduce MillBill, an agent built on this separation. Given B-rep part, its stock and its material, MillBill recognises machining features with graph neural network on the B-rep [48] and chooses setups among the six axis-aligned orientations of indexed three-axis machining. The language model then revises standard-practice reference of operations, tools and cutting parameters derived from the features, the tool library and cutting-data model; its tools MillBill: Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback PREPRINT must exist in the library and its cutting data are clamped to the machine limits. geometric harness CAM toolpath generation, material-removal simulation and surface-deviation measurement turns the plan into G-code, simulates the cut and attributes deviations from the design to features and operations. It corrects what it can, for example by adding rest finishing, returns the remaining deviations to the model, and keeps the best of at most three builds. Setups are chosen by what the available cutters can reach, not by visibility alone: deep, narrow region can be visible yet out of reach once the holder is taken into account. Accessibility has been computed before [22, 37]; MillBill screens the whole tool library with one height-map dilation per remaining pair of holder overhang and reach, after removing redundant pairs, picks setups greedily and plans each on the stock the simulated earlier setups leave. We evaluate on 100 parts collected from GrabCAD and score every system by simulating its G-code. With the open Qwen3.8-27B model [40], MillBill leaves 97.4% of the target surface within 0.1 mm, against 94.3% for the best code-writing agent built on frontier model, GPT-6 Astra [38]. Most of the gain comes from the harness: without the model, it already reaches 97.0%. Our contributions are: MillBill, B-rep-to-G-code pipeline in which language model makes the machining decisions and geometric harness executes and verifies them (Sec. 3); an open benchmark of 4,294 GrabCAD parts paired with milling stocks, with protocol that scores any planners G-code in simulation (Sec. 4.1); state-of-the-art results on this benchmark with locally hosted open model, which outperforms code-writing agents built on frontier models (Sec. 4).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Machining feature recognition. Learned machining feature recognition moved from voxel grids [56] to graphs on the B-rep [11, 12], alongside general B-rep encoders [23, 32]. AAGNet segments geometric attributed adjacency graph into feature classes, instances and bottom faces in one network and introduced the MFInstSeg dataset [48]; later work uses transformers, domain adaptation, self-supervised pretraining or panoptic segmentation [13, 16, 50, 54]. Vision language models prompted with renderings can also name features, but produce spurious labels [28]. Recognition is not our contribution: MillBill uses AAGNet for instance segmentation and measures feature dimensions on the B-rep. Process planning, setups and simulation. Computer-aided process planning has long history of rule-based, knowledge-based and optimisation-based systems [49], and fully automatic planning remains open [4]. Setup planning is commonly posed through visibility, using visibility maps on the Gaussian sphere [47] or global visibility maps computed from slices of the part [20]. Accessibility cones that account for the tool and holder have been computed for 3+2-axis milling [22], configuration-space formulations derive the volume each tool can remove [10, 37], and cutter selection has been posed as trade-off between accessible area and machining time [52]. MillBill applies holder-aware reach test for the whole tool library, one height-map dilation per remaining pair of holder overhang and reach, after removing redundant pairs, and selects indexed setups greedily by the material they newly make reachable rather than by visibility. To verify programs, material-removal simulation represents the workpiece with Z-maps [6], dexels [46, 55] or voxels [25, 43] and removes the swept volume of the tool [2]; MillBill instead tests query points exactly against the analytically swept cutters, without discretising the workpiece, and uses dexel height maps only to localise the deviations it feeds back to the planner. Language models for manufacturing and CAM. Language models have been surveyed and evaluated across manufacturing tasks [34]. For process planning, CAPP-GPT generates process plans with GPT-style framework [8] and ARKNESS grounds an LLM in machining knowledge graphs so that small local model answers process-planning questions [19]. Design-to-Plan coordinates LLM agents that plan from 3D CAD models and 2D drawings [29]; like the planners above, it stops before toolpaths, so its plans are never executed or checked against the geometry. Other work has the model write machine code: GLLM generates G-code with fine-tuned model and corrects it with validation feedback [3], general-purpose chat models have been compared on writing G-code for three-axis part [45], and neuro-symbolic approach constrains LLM G-code generation with separation-logic verification [33]; related studies have models debug G-code for additive manufacturing [24] or verify it against machine screens [18]. CNCGEN, closest to our setting, learns operations and toolpaths from B-rep models on large machining dataset [57]; MillBill needs no training on machining plans or toolpaths: an off-the-shelf open model makes the decisions, pretrained feature recogniser segments the part, and geometric algorithms execute and verify them. We do not compare with CNCGEN: it is trained on its own dataset, outputs operations and parameterised toolpaths rather than G-code, and, to our knowledge, 2 MillBill: Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback PREPRINT Figure 1. MillBill overview. The language model revises standard-practice machining plan; the geometric harness executes it, simulates the result and returns its deviations from the design. (1) The target B-rep. (2) AAGNet labels each face with machining feature class (Sec. 3.1). (3) Setups are chosen among the six axis directions by what the cutters can reach (Sec. 3.2). (4) The model revises the operations, tools and cutting parameters of each setup, within the tool library and the machine limits (Sec. 3.3). (5) The harness writes the toolpaths and G-code (Sec. 3.4). (6) The simulated workpiece is compared with the design (blue: excess material, grey: within 0.1 mm, red: gouge), and the deviations go back to the agent (Secs. 3.5 and 3.6). its code and models are not publicly available. CNC-Net learns without supervision to reproduce shape with milling and drilling operations of cylindrical tools [53]. Tool-using agents with execution feedback. Language-model agents learn to call tools [42], interleave reasoning with actions [51], and improve their outputs from feedback, whether self-generated or from execution [35, 44]. In CAD, learned models write CAD programs from point clouds and images [15, 27, 31], and agents generate and edit models through CAD kernels [9, 17, 21, 36, 41] and refine them from rendered or measured results [5, 9, 26, 36]. MillBill applies this pattern to machining, where the feedback is the deviation of the simulated part from the design rather than the appearance or validity of model.

sections.title: 3 MillBill
sections.content: Problem. The input is target part given as B-rep (STEP), stock P, workpiece material and, optionally, drawing notes such as threads, fits and surface-finish requirements. The stock is either user-supplied blank or the bounding box of the part enlarged by fixed allowances. The machine is three-axis vertical machining centre with library of cutters and machine profile (spindle speed, feed, power and torque limits). The part may be machined in several indexed setups, each approaching it from one of the six axis directions = {x, y, z}. The output is one G-code program per setup. program is judged by the part it produces: after simulating all setups, we measure the fraction of the target surface that lies within tolerance τ of the design (Sec. 3.5). Overview. MillBill splits the work between language model and geometric harness  (Fig. 1)  . The harness recognises machining features on the B-rep (Sec. 3.1) and chooses setups by tool reachability (Sec. 3.2). For each setup, the agent retrieves machining knowledge and decides the operation sequence, tools and cutting parameters (Sec. 3.3). The harness turns the plan into toolpaths and G-code (Sec. 3.4), simulates material removal and measures the result against the target (Sec. 3.5), and returns the deviations so that the plan can be refined (Sec. 3.6). The model never writes coordinates or G-code: every toolpath is generated by the harness, and every program is verified in simulation.

sections.title: 3.1 Machining features
sections.content: Machining decisions are made per feature, so the part is first segmented into machining features with AAGNet [48]. AAGNet operates on geometric attributed adjacency graph of the B-rep, whose nodes are faces and whose edges are shared B-rep edges, and predicts in one pass semantic class for every face, face-to-face affinity that groups faces into 3 MillBill: Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback PREPRINT feature instances, and which faces form the bottom of feature. We use the network trained on MFInstSeg [48], whose 24 classes cover holes, passages, slots, steps, pockets, chamfers, rounds and O-rings, plus stock class. Faces predicted to belong to one feature are grouped, each face into at most one group; group takes the class with the highest summed face scores, and stock groups are dropped. The network determines which faces form feature and what type it is; its dimensions are measured on the B-rep. AAGNet and FreeCAD load the STEP model independently, so their face indices may differ; each predicted face is matched to the FreeCAD face with the nearest centroid, within tolerances on centroid distance and area. For hole, coaxial concave cylindrical faces give the diameter, the depth along the axis, whether it is through or blind, and the shape of its bottom; coaxial stacks become counterbores or countersinks. For pockets, slots and steps, the predicted bottom faces give the floor, from which we measure the floor height, depth, extent, minimum width and the smallest concave corner radius, and the class determines whether the feature is open to the side. Features whose floor faces away from the current setup are left to another setup. Drawing notes are parsed by the language model into structured annotations (threads, tolerance grades, surface roughness, counts and locations), which are then matched to features. Each annotationfeature pair is scored as = wtype stype + wdim sdim + wloc sloc, (1) where stype checks that the annotation applies to the feature type, sdim compares annotated and measured dimensions (e.g., thread matches hole at its tap-drill or clearance diameter), and sloc matches spatial keywords such as top or blind. Confident unique matches are accepted directly; ambiguous ones are resolved by the model, which may assign one annotation to several features. Matched annotations set how feature is machined: threaded hole gets thread-cutting operation, and hole tighter than drilling can hold is reamed or bored after drilling.

sections.title: 3.2 Reach-aware setup planning
sections.content: A region of the part can be machined from direction only if cutter can get there. Visibility from is necessary but not sufficient: cutter has finite length and is clamped in holder much wider than itself, so deep, narrow region may be visible yet out of reach. We discretise the volume to be removed, P, into voxels and, for each direction, call voxel visible if no part material lies above it along d. Let Hd(x, y) be the height of the parts top surface in the frame of d. Each milling cutter with radius rt and usable length Lt (overall length minus the clamped length), held in holder of radius rh, overhangs its own axis by ρt = rh rt. visible voxel at (x, y, z) is reachable from if some cutter clears the part around it: : max (x,y)(x,y)ρt Hd(x, y) Lt. (2) Equation (2) is necessary condition for holder clearance: it checks disk of radius ρt around the voxel, not the full holder around every admissible tool axis, so it can accept regions the holder would collide with. cutter is skipped if another has at least the same usable length Lt and no larger holder overhang ρt, since every voxel it reaches is also reached by the other. For each remaining (ρt, Lt) pair, the maximum part height within disk of radius ρt around every height-map cell is computed once, as grey-scale dilation of Hd, which tests Eq. (2) for all voxels at once. Holes are assigned by visibility along the drilling direction, assuming sufficient drill reach; drill diameter and length are checked during tool selection. Setups are chosen greedily. The primary setup is the direction that reaches the largest volume of material to be removed, with preference for +z when it is nearly as good. Further directions are added in order of the reachable volume they newly expose, until the gain falls below small threshold or all six directions are used. feature is assigned to setup if most of its volume is reachable from it and not yet removed by earlier setups; features that no direction reaches are reported, and so is the unreachable volume. Each later setup is planned on the stock that the earlier setups actually leave, as measured by the simulation of Sec. 3.5.

sections.title: 3.3 Machining decisions by the agent
sections.content: A language model revises the machining plan in three stages, following the agent architecture of Design-to-Plan [29], each ReAct agent [51] that alternates reasoning with calls to harness tools and ends with structured JSON answer. Knowledge retrieval runs once per part. For each setup, the harness prepares an initial plan: standard-practice operation sequence, the cutters that pass geometric and material checks, and cutting data from physical model. The process-sequence agent revises the operations and their order, and the tool-selection agent the tools and cutting parameters. 4 MillBill: Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback PREPRINT Knowledge retrieval. From the recognised features, their dimensions and the workpiece material, the first agent retrieves machining limits and recommendations, such as minimum internal corner radii, maximum hole depth-todiameter ratios and material-specific cutting guidance, and flags violations (conflicts with these guidelines, not simulated defects); e.g., hole deeper than the recommended ratio is flagged for the planning agents when they choose the drilling process and tool. Three sub-agents search textual guidelines, rule and thread tables, featurematerial tables, process knowledge graph and materials database in parallel; their results are merged, keeping the highest severity of conflict, into rules, violations and recommended processes for the other two agents. Process sequence. The second agent decides which operations machine each feature and in what order. It sees the features, the matched annotations, the retrieved violations and recommendations, and reference sequence that follows standard shop practice: datum faces first, then roughing of all features, finishing, hole making from spot drilling through drilling, chamfering or countersinking, reaming or boring to tapping, and deburring last. Its tools look up process capabilities, retrieve sequencing rules and validate candidate sequence against hard precedence constraints (paired operations on the same feature, nested features, roughing before finishing). The proposed sequence is normalised to the process catalogue, minimally repaired by moving only the steps that violate hard constraint, and accepted if it has no more critical violations than the reference. Tools and cutting parameters. The third agent assigns cutter and cutting parameters to every operation. Candidate cutters are filtered in four stages: whether the process needs tool, which tool categories serve it, which cutters are rated for the materials ISO 513 group and fit the feature geometry (e.g., diameter below the slot width or corner radius, sufficient reach and flute length, drill diameter and length, tap thread series), and ranking that prefers the largest cutter that fits. Reference cutting data come from physical model: cutting speed from the material group and tool material, feed per tooth proportional to the cutter diameter with chip-thinning compensation at small radial engagement, depths of cut by strategy, and spindle power from the Kienzle force model, limited by the machine [30]. The agent can change the tool, which must exist in the library with valid cutting data, and can adjust spindle speed, feed and depths of cut; speed and feed are clamped to the machine limits. Operations of the same tool within phase are then grouped to avoid tool changes, provided no precedence constraint is broken.

sections.title: 3.4 Toolpaths and G-code
sections.content: The harness executes the plan in the CAM workbench of FreeCAD [1]. Each setup becomes CAM job on the part rotated so that the setup direction points up, with its stock and one tool controller per combination of cutter and cutting parameters. Facing, adaptive clearing of suitable closed pockets, outer profiling and drilling cycles use FreeCAD operations. Slots, steps, other pockets, cavity roughing and surface finishing use toolpaths computed by the harness on height map of the target seen from the setup direction. Roughing paths keep the tool centre above the target dilated by the tool disk, which makes them gouge-free for flat cutters by construction, and proceed in levels at the chosen depth of cut. Finishing paths follow waterlines obtained from an exact Euclidean distance transform of the material at each level [39], with raster pass on sloped regions. Counterbores and thread milling use helical paths. Every path computed by the harness passes through gouge check against dexel height map of the target, and any piece of move that would cut into the target is lifted. FreeCADs post-processor writes the G-code; canned cycles that are unsafe in its generic output are rewritten, and safety check flags unsafe moves (Sec. S1).

To localise errors for the feedback, the harness additionally keeps dexel height map of each setup [6, 46]: connected regions of out-of-tolerance excess or gouge are attributed to the feature they lie on and to the last operation that cut there. Regions that no library cutter can resolve, such as sharp internal corners below the smallest cutter radius or depths beyond the longest reach, are labelled as inherent and are not fed back as errors.

sections.title: 3.6 Refinement from geometric feedback
sections.content: After each build, the harness ranks the result by safety issues, gouged area and the score of Eq. (5), and keeps the best build seen so far. If the result is out of tolerance, the harness first adds rest finishing: it locates material left above the target, selects up to two library cutters that can reach and finish it, and machines it with parallel back-and-forth passes spaced so that the ridges left between passes are at most τ /4 high. Defects that have direct correction, such as an empty toolpath or finishing allowance with no finishing pass, are corrected by the harness. The remaining defects are returned to the model together with the operations, the features and the attributed error regions, and the model proposes minimal set of fixes from fixed action space: switch the tool of an operation, set the finishing allowance, the final depth, the depth of cut, the stepover or the peck depth, or drop finishing, deburring or spot-drilling operation. Each fix is validated (e.g., switched tool must exist in the library with valid cutting data, finishing allowance must lie in 01 mm) but not bounded relative to the reference. The plan is rebuilt and re-verified, for at most three builds, and the loop stops early when build is within tolerance or no longer improves.

sections.title: 4.1 Setup
sections.content: Parts. We evaluate on 100 parts drawn from collection of 4,294 models selected at random from the GrabCAD Community Library1, used under the GrabCAD Terms of Use (Sec. S2). The collection pairs every single-solid STEP part with milling stock. For 1,396 parts the stock is turned: 694 stepped shafts with 1 mm of allowance, and 702 solids of revolution with no allowance, their local cavities filled out to the circumscribed circle. The other 2,898 stocks are prismatic: stepped casting, forging or profile, or rolled flat bar, square bar, plate, plate strip or sheet (Sec. S2). The 100 parts are stratified draw from this collection (random seed 2026): ten parts with turned stock and ten from each of the eight prismatic stock kinds, then ten more from the remaining candidates. candidate is one solid with 25 to 200 B-rep faces, at most 0.5% of the removal volume that no three-axis cutter reaches from any of the six axis-aligned directions, and workpiece material from the knowledge base (Sec. S2); near-duplicate shapes are dropped, which removes 112 candidates. The draw yields 10 to 13 parts of each kind. Each task consists of the part as STEP B-rep, the stock paired with it in the collection and the workpiece material (Sec. 3). The parts range from 5.08 to 1,840 mm along the longest bounding-box edge and from 25 to 179 B-rep faces, 90 of them require more than one setup  (Fig. 2)  . Six parts are longer than the travel of typical three-axis machining centre (600 400 450 mm); we keep them, since the harness does not check machine travel. Their scores are in Sec. S4. Unless stated otherwise, the tolerance is τ = 0.1 mm and all systems use the machine profile and tool library of Tab. S2. Baselines. Code-writing frontier agents receive the same task as MillBill: the part and stock as STEP files, the material, the notes, the tolerance, the machine profile, the coordinate convention and the tool library, and must return one G-code program per setup together with description of its tools and operations (Sec. S3). The model reads the STEP files and writes the G-code itself: it can run Python, view images and read and write files, and so write and execute its own geometry and toolpath code. We build such agents on GPT-6 Astra [38] and Claude Opus 5.5 [7], each with budget of $2 and at most 80 turns per part and no feedback on its programs, and on Qwen3.8-27B [40], the same model as in MillBill, which runs locally with at most 160 calls and four hours per part and receives two rounds of 1https://grabcad.com/library 6 MillBill: Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback PREPRINT Figure 2. sections.title: 4.3 Ablations
sections.content: Table 2 removes one component at time. Reference plan executes the standard-practice reference of Sec. 3.3 without the language model, which separates the contribution of the model from that of the harness. Fixed +z setup replaces the reach-aware setups of Sec. 3.2 with single setup from +z. Executed without the language model (including knowledge retrieval) but with the harness corrections and repair rounds, the reference plan already leaves 97.0% of the surface within tolerance; the model raises this to 97.4% (paired difference 0.35 pp, 95% bootstrap CI [0.09, 0.68]; better on 43 parts, worse on 23) and reduces the gouged area from 0.77% to 0.54%. This reduction comes from the ten single-setup parts: on the 90 multi-setup parts the gouged area is 0.46% with the model and 0.45% without it. sections.content: Refinement rounds. With budget of one build, MillBill leaves 95.6% of the surface within tolerance; second build raises this to 97.2% and third to 97.4% (Fig. 4a); Fig. 4b shows how many builds the 430 setups use. sections.title: 5 Limitations
sections.content: MillBill is limited to indexed three-axis machining from the six principal directions; parts that need inclined setups or simultaneous five-axis motion are out of scope. Workholding and machine travel are not modelled: setups are chosen by tool accessibility, not by whether the part can be clamped, the toolpaths are not checked for collisions with fixtures or the tool holder (Eq. (2) is only necessary condition for holder clearance), and parts exceeding the machine travel are not rejected. The geometric simulation does not account for tool deflection, vibration or wear. As result, toolpath that meets tolerance requirements in simulation may fail to achieve them during machining. Taps and thread mills are also not simulated, meaning that thread geometry is planned but not verified. The knowledge base holds representative, not vendor-specific, cutting data, and AAGNet is trained on synthetic parts, so recognition errors on real parts can propagate into the plan, though the simulation catches their geometric effects. We evaluate on 100 parts from one public library, one run per method and part.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced MillBill, an agent that turns B-rep part into G-code by separating machining decisions from geometric execution. locally hosted language model refines an initial plan of operations, tools and cutting parameters. geometric harness recognises features, selects setups by tool accessibility, generates every toolpath, simulates the cut and reports deviations per feature and operation, so the model never computes coordinates. With 27B open model, MillBill achieves 97.4% of the target surface within 0.1 mm on 100 parts, against 94.3% for the best code-writing frontier agent; the initial plan without the model reaches 97.0%. The same simulator can score any planners G-code. Future work includes five-axis setups, workholding and verification of threads and surface finish. sections.title: Implementation details
sections.content: Language model and agents. All agents use Qwen3.8-27B [40] served locally with vLLM through an OpenAIcompatible interface, in FP8 on four NVIDIA H100 80 GB GPUs with tensor parallelism of four, with 250,000-token context (54.6 calls per part on average on the benchmark), at temperature 0 with thinking disabled. Structured answers are requested in JSON mode and retried up to twice if they do not parse. Each ReAct agent [51] has fixed iteration budget (Tab. S2); on the last iteration tools are withheld so that the model must answer. Identical repeated tool calls return the cached result with warning, and turn consisting only of repeated calls forces the final answer. Tool results are truncated to 3,500 characters in the conversation. Knowledge retrieval runs three sub-agents concurrently (text and knowledge graph; SQL, tables and decision tree; materials database), whose outputs are merged deterministically and summarised by coordinator call. Knowledge base. The knowledge base contains 17 workpiece materials with ISO 513 groups and Kienzle constants, 26 machining rules and 37 thread specifications (ISO 261, ASME B1.1) in SQL tables, 55 featurematerial rows, 23 sections of machining guidelines retrieved by BM25, and knowledge graph of 103 triples over processes, features and materials. The tool library has 75 cutters: 30 flat, 7 ball and 5 bull-nose end mills, 5 face mills, 5 twist drills, 4 spot drills, 6 countersinks, 3 chamfer mills, 3 taps, 3 thread mills, 2 reamers and 2 boring bars. Feature recognition. AAGNet [48] runs in its own environment with the authors MFInstSeg weights. Instance affinities and bottom-face probabilities are thresholded at 0.5. predicted face is matched to CAD-kernel face if their centroids are within 0.05 mm + 103 times the part scale and their areas within 1%. Table S1 lists how MFInstSeg classes map to the feature types used in planning.
